title: API requests, responses, and JSON
principle: An API is a contract between a caller and a service.
paragraphs: A client sends a request to a service endpoint. The request names an operation and carries data. The service checks the request, performs an operation, and returns a response.
JSON is a text format for structured data. It uses named fields, values, arrays, and nested objects. A model request can use JSON to carry a model identifier, messages, and settings.

A successful network response confirms that the service handled the request. It does not prove that the generated answer is correct. The caller must inspect the response, error state, and task result.

title: IAM identities, roles, policies, and explicit deny
principle: An identity names who or what makes a request. A policy states which actions that identity may take.
paragraphs: An IAM role is an identity that a trusted user or service can assume. A workload can use temporary role credentials to call AWS services.
A policy is a JSON permission document. It can allow or deny actions on resources under conditions. An explicit deny blocks an action, even when another policy allows it.
Use separate roles for workloads with different duties. Grant only the actions and resources that each role needs. Model instructions do not replace IAM authorization.

title: Regions, Availability Zones, VPCs, and endpoints
principle: A Region is a geographic AWS area. A VPC is a virtual network in one Region.
paragraphs: An Availability Zone is an isolated location within a Region. A VPC can use subnets in multiple Availability Zones. This lets a design place resources across separate locations in one Region.
An endpoint gives a workload a path to a service. An interface VPC endpoint uses AWS PrivateLink to connect a VPC privately to supported AWS services.

Private connectivity does not grant permission by itself. IAM and endpoint policies still control allowed requests. Cross-Region inference can route work across Regions, so check the data-location rules before use.

title: S3 objects and encryption keys
principle: Amazon S3 stores objects in buckets. Encryption protects data at rest and in transit under configured service controls.
paragraphs: An S3 object contains data and metadata. A bucket stores objects under keys. Applications use the bucket and key to identify a source file or result file.
A knowledge base can read source files and metadata from storage, then create derived chunks and embeddings. The source object remains distinct from its search index.

AWS Key Management Service manages cryptographic keys used by supported encryption features. Access to encrypted data can depend on both storage permission and permission to use the key. Protect keys and source data with scoped access.

title: Lambda, containers, queues, and workflows
principle: Compute runs code. A queue stores work for later processing. A workflow controls a sequence of steps.
paragraphs: AWS Lambda runs a function when an event or request invokes it. A container packages code and its runtime dependencies. A service such as Amazon ECS can run container workloads.
A queue such as Amazon SQS holds messages until a consumer processes them. This separates the producer from the worker and supports asynchronous work.

A workflow service coordinates steps, decisions, retries, and state. Use it when the application needs an explicit sequence or branch. Choose a compute pattern from task duration, runtime needs, and operations.

title: Training, inference, and embeddings
principle: Training changes or creates model parameters. Inference uses a model to produce an output. Embedding converts content to a vector representation.
paragraphs: A foundation model learns patterns during training. Customization can use additional data to improve behavior for a task. Training and customization require controlled data and evaluation.
Inference is a model call at application time. The request supplies a prompt or messages. The model returns generated content. Inference does not automatically update model parameters.

An embedding model maps text or other supported content into a vector. A retrieval system compares query and document vectors to find candidates. Similarity is a search signal, not proof that a passage is true.
